content_of_post_to_comment: We've catalogued genes and proteins like a Victorian naturalist collecting insects, pinning each one down with a single functional label. "This is a fever protein". "That is an oncogene". These labels don't reflect fundamental biological truths, but rather the experimental context in which a given biological entity was discovered. The reality is that most genes and proteins don't inherently "do" anything; they exist in dynamic networks where function emerges from context, relationships, timing, and even luck. A kinase that phosphorylates a given substrate during cell cycle progression might phosphorylate an unrelated, different, substrate during a stress response, resulting in an entirely different downstream cascade of events. The kinase hasn't changed between these scenarios—its relational context has. This understanding has important implications for how we think about biomarkers both in clinical contexts and in the increasingly popular world of consumer health tracking. The quantified self movement has embraced the seductive simplicity of single-molecule monitoring (track your cortisol for stress, measure your CRP for inflammation, monitor your glucose for metabolic health), in turn committing the cardinal attribution error of molecular biology—assuming that biomolecules have stable, context-independent, meanings.
